frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence (as of early 2014) to justify HRA Pharma investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its ulipristal acetate emergency contraceptive (ellaOne).
constraints: Limited to public sources available before early 2014; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must address consumer demand, willingness to pay, competitive landscape, regulatory status, and potential impact on existing prescription sales.
Any recommendation must be based on observable demand, market trends, or competitive evidence, not speculation.
alternatives: 1) Develop a dedicated consumer brand for emergency contraception (e.g., a consumer‑focused product line).
2) Expand the existing prescription model by offering a consumer‑friendly version of ellaOne through retail pharmacies or online channels.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on prescription sales to doctors and hospitals.
4) License the ulipristal technology to third‑party manufacturers for consumer products, capturing value through royalties.
5) Partner with consumer health brands to co‑develop and market an emergency contraceptive product, sharing distribution and branding.

T1.claim: Women will adopt an emergency contraceptive sold directly in pharmacies because they view it as a private health product, and they will pay a premium for convenience and discreet access.
T1.who_benefits: Women seeking emergency contraception and pharmacies that can stock and sell it without a prescription.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: If the product is available behind the counter, women avoid the stigma of a doctor visit and can purchase it privately, leading them to choose it over a prescription-only option.
T1.how_value_is_captured: HRA Pharma captures value through higher per-unit sales in pharmacies and potential premium pricing for a consumer-branded product.
assumptions: Women in target markets perceive emergency contraception as a private health issue rather than a medical necessity requiring a doctor.
Pharmacies are willing to stock and promote a consumer-branded product.
Regulatory status allows non-prescription distribution without compromising safety.
predictions: In markets where emergency contraception is currently prescription-only, women will show higher purchase intent when offered a non-prescription version.
Pharmacies will report increased sales of a consumer-branded product compared to a generic levonorgestrel pill.
Willingness to pay will be higher for a branded product than for an unbranded generic.
T1.first_claim: Women will adopt an emergency contraceptive sold directly in pharmacies because they view it as a private health product, and they will pay a premium for convenience and discreet access.

T2.claim: Women will adopt an emergency contraceptive sold directly in pharmacies because they trust the brand and regulatory status of a product already approved without prescription, leading them to choose it over a generic levonorgestrel pill.
T2.who_benefits: Women who value brand reliability and regulatory clearance, and pharmacies that stock a trusted product.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: If a product is already available without prescription and has a proven safety record, women are less likely to seek a prescription or a generic alternative, resulting in higher purchase frequency.
T2.how_value_is_captured: HRA Pharma captures value through higher repeat purchases of a branded product and potential premium pricing justified by brand trust.
assumptions: Women in target markets associate brand approval with safety and efficacy.
Regulatory status of a prescription-only product transfers to a non-prescription version.
Pharmacies will stock a trusted brand over a generic levonorgestrel pill.
predictions: In markets where emergency contraception is prescription-only, women will show higher purchase intent for a branded product compared to a generic levonorgestrel pill.
Pharmacies will report higher sales volume for a branded product than for an unbranded generic.
Willingness to pay will be lower for a generic levonorgestrel pill than for a branded product.

T1.claim: Homeowners and small businesses will adopt Atlas Copco consumer vacuum pumps if they perceive them as reliable, portable, and easy to use for tasks like cleaning, moving, and small trades, because they value convenience and safety.
T1.who_benefits: Homeowners and small business owners who need a reliable vacuum for occasional heavy-duty tasks.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: They currently use consumer-grade vacuums that are heavy, cumbersome, or lack power; a consumer-grade vacuum that is lightweight, portable, and easy to operate would change their choice from a consumer vacuum to a professional-grade vacuum.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Atlas Copco would sell premium-priced consumer vacuum pumps directly to consumers through retail channels, capturing higher margins than industrial vacuum pumps.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a vacuum that is significantly lighter and easier to handle than standard consumer vacuums.
Retail distribution channels exist for Atlas Copco consumer vacuum pumps.
Marketing can effectively communicate the convenience and safety benefits to consumers.
predictions: In a test offering a consumer vacuum pump to homeowners, purchase intent or actual purchase will be higher than for a comparable industrial vacuum pump.
Surveyed consumers will rank convenience and portability as top reasons for choosing a vacuum.

X1.name: Residential Elevator Purchase Intent Test
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.
X1.sample: 400 homeowners (200 in a rapidly urbanizing region like India/Southeast Asia and 200 in a developed region like North America/Europe) recruited via a panel.
X1.measure: 1) Percentage of respondents indicating intent to purchase a residential elevator within 12 weeks. 2) Average WTP per unit (in euros).

prediction_by_theory.T1: At least 30% of homeowners in the developed region will express intent to purchase, and average WTP will be at least 20% above the baseline price.
prediction_by_theory.T2: At least 40% of building owners in the developed region will place a contract within 12 weeks, and contract value will be at least 30% higher than a standard elevator purchase.

X1.decision_rule: If the developed-market intent threshold is met (>=30%) and WTP is >=20% above baseline, proceed to develop a consumer proposition. If the buildingowner-contract threshold is met (>=40% contract intent) and contract value is >=30% higher, invest in lifecycle services. If neither is met, no expansion.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. The evidence does not show whether building owners purchase elevators as a consumer requirement versus a service contract, and willingness to pay for residential elevators is unproven. Continue focusing on existing B2B markets and lifecycle services.
final.target_customer: Building owners, facility managers, and real estate developers in cities who value capability and require lifecycle services for elevators and escalators.
final.value_proposition: Deepen lifecycle services, predictive maintenance, and compliance support to reduce downtime and ensure regulatory compliance, earning recurring revenue and deeper integration with building management systems.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Residential Elevator Purchase Intent Test (400 homeowners, 12 weeks, €18,000) to validate demand and willingness to pay before any investment.
final.uncertainty: The size of the residential elevator market and the willingness to pay for a differentiated consumer product are unknown. Regulatory requirements for residential elevators may also limit consumer purchases.
would_change_if: If the test shows at least 30% of homeowners in the developed region express intent to purchase and willingness to pay is at least 20% above baseline, we would consider developing a consumer proposition.
If the test shows at least 40% of building owners place contracts and contract value is at least 30% higher than a standard purchase, we would invest in lifecycle services.
If new evidence shows strong consumer demand for residential elevators or significant willingness to pay, we would reassess the investment case.

position.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Public evidence shows Alfa Laval already markets hygienic equipment and process expertise to home-care manufacturers and sells under its own brand, but it does not demonstrate consumer willingness to pay a premium for safety or sustainability. A proposed test (Consumer Messaging Test) is needed to validate demand before committing resources.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Alfa Laval investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current industrial B2B offerings.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must demonstrate consumer demand, willingness to pay, and a viable route to market for a differentiated product.
Any recommendation must consider Alfa Laval’s existing B2B presence and current reach to individual buyers.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home water filtration, small‑scale food processing, marine recreational equipment).
2) Expand the existing B2B product portfolio with new industrial features or services without creating a separate consumer brand.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on current industrial customers and existing B2B channels.
4) Partner with or license technology to consumer brands rather than selling under Alfa Laval brand.
5) Target a new customer segment (e.g., small‑to‑medium home‑care manufacturers) with a tailored offering.

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer product if they perceive it as a premium, safety‑enhancing solution that addresses a specific pain point (e.g., water purity, hygiene, or convenience). Alfa Laval can capture value by selling under its own brand at premium prices, leveraging its existing B2B reputation and distribution.
T1.who_benefits: Consumers seeking higher‑quality, trusted water or hygiene products; Alfa Laval gains premium revenue and brand extension.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Growing consumer awareness of water quality issues and demand for hygienic, green products creates willingness to pay more for proven safety and performance.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Alfa Laval sells differentiated consumer products directly or through retail partners at premium margins, using its existing B2B channels to reach individual buyers.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for safety and performance in consumer water products.
Alfa Laval can adapt its industrial expertise to meet consumer expectations without compromising quality.
Retail or direct‑to‑consumer channels are accessible to reach individual buyers.
predictions: A survey of target consumers will show >30% would purchase a differentiated water filtration product at a price 20% above standard options.
Sales of a consumer product will be concentrated in regions with high water‑quality concerns (e.g., developed markets with aging infrastructure).

X1.name: Consumer Messaging Test: Premium vs. Green Positioning
X1.method: Online survey with randomized exposure to two product concepts: (1) Premium safety positioning (e.g., "Alfa Laval water filtration: proven safety, reduced risk, trusted brand"). (2) Green sustainability positioning (e.g., "Alfa Laval eco‑filtered water: sustainable, eco‑friendly, environmentally responsible"). Participants are randomly assigned to view one concept and then asked about willingness to pay (WTP) and intent to purchase at a price 20% above standard options.
X1.sample: 400 U.S. adults (200 per group) who have expressed interest in home water filtration or home care products, recruited via an online panel.
X1.measure: Average WTP (in euros) and purchase intent (1‑10 scale) for each positioning.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Premium positioning will generate higher WTP and purchase intent than green positioning, because safety‑enhancing messaging is perceived as a premium value.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Green positioning will generate higher WTP and purchase intent than premium positioning, because sustainability aligns with environmental values and creates perceived eco‑friendly advantage.

X1.decision_rule: If the average WTP for premium positioning exceeds green positioning by at least €5 (a 20% price premium) and the difference is statistically significant (p < 0.05), proceed to develop a premium‑focused consumer proposition. If green positioning’s WTP is at least €5 above premium and the difference is statistically significant, develop a green‑focused consumer proposition. If neither condition is met, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Public evidence shows Alfa Laval already markets hygienic equipment and process expertise to home-care manufacturers and sells under its own brand, but it does not demonstrate consumer willingness to pay a premium for safety or sustainability. A proposed test (Consumer Messaging Test) is needed to validate demand before committing resources.
final.target_customer: Home-care manufacturers and individual consumers seeking hygienic, safety‑enhancing water or hygiene products.
final.value_proposition: A differentiated consumer product that leverages Alfa Laval’s industrial expertise to deliver proven safety, hygiene, and performance, sold under the Alfa Laval brand at premium margins.
final.next_action: Run the Consumer Messaging Test (400 U.S. adults, two positioning groups, 20% price premium, 6‑week timeline, €15,000 budget) to measure willingness to pay and purchase intent.
final.uncertainty: Consumer willingness to pay a premium for safety and performance; competitive landscape of existing consumer water filtration brands; ability to adapt industrial expertise to consumer messaging without compromising quality.
would_change_if: The test shows green positioning generates at least €5 higher WTP than premium positioning and the difference is statistically significant, indicating strong sustainability demand.

constraints: Limited to publicly available information; no internal company data.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Eppendorf investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B offerings.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeframe for any proposed experiment.
Revenue of €924 million in 2025 sold through three Commercial Units; no consumer/retail sales reported.
Uncertainty about current reach to individual buyers and existing consumer demand.
Need to identify a specific use case with clear consumer need and Eppendorf’s ability to differentiate and capture value.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home DIY lab, small business, or a niche professional segment).
2) Expand into adjacent B2B segments with existing products (e.g., add new consumables or accessories to existing lab instrument lines).
3) No expansion – continue focusing exclusively on academic and industrial research labs.
4) Change the route to market (e.g., direct-to-consumer online sales, partnerships with retailers, or subscription model) without altering product offering.

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt Eppendorf instruments for home DIY labs if they perceive the tools as reliable, safe, and easy to use, and if they can purchase them directly online at a premium price.
T1.who_benefits: Home DIY lab enthusiasts and small businesses seeking professional-grade equipment for personal or small-scale experiments.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Growing interest in home science and DIY projects creates a demand for accessible, high-quality lab tools; consumers will purchase when they trust the brand and can buy without lab equipment expertise.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Eppendorf would sell premium-priced instruments and consumables directly to consumers online, capturing margin through brand reputation and direct-to-consumer sales.
assumptions: Consumers currently lack access to Eppendorf products outside academic/industrial labs.
Online purchase channels can reach and serve home DIY users effectively.
Consumers are willing to pay a premium for reliability and brand trust.
predictions: A survey of home DIY users would show >30% indicating intent to purchase Eppendorf instruments at a price 20% above standard lab prices.
Online sales of consumer-facing Eppendorf products would generate at least €1 million in revenue within 12 months of launch.

T2.claim: Consumers will adopt Eppendorf instruments for small businesses and professional home use if they need reliable, high-throughput lab equipment for commercial or professional applications, and if Eppendorf can provide training, support, and a subscription model to reduce ongoing costs.
T2.who_benefits: Small businesses, professional home users, and professional labs that require consistent, high-quality equipment for regular use.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Professional users face recurring costs for consumables and maintenance; a subscription or training model lowers upfront and ongoing expenses, making Eppendorf instruments more attractive than one-time purchases.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Eppendorf would sell instruments at a premium with subscription or training services, capturing recurring revenue and building long-term customer relationships.
assumptions: Professional users currently purchase lab equipment through one-time purchases or through third-party distributors.
A subscription or training model can be implemented without significant product redesign.
Professional users are willing to pay a premium for reliability and support.
predictions: A survey of professional home users would show >30% indicating intent to subscribe to a subscription service for Eppendorf instruments at a monthly fee of €30.
Subscription sign-ups would generate at least €500,000 in recurring revenue within the first year.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Getinge investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current hospital and lab sales.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeframe for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and a viable route to market for a new consumer product.
Any recommendation must be based on observable demand, not assumptions.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home ventilator for at‑home care).
2) Expand into adjacent B2B segments with existing products (e.g., add consumer reprocessing kits for small clinics).
3) No expansion: continue focusing on current hospital and lab markets.
4) License existing products to consumer brands for white‑label distribution.
5) Partner with consumer brands to co‑develop and market a new product under a consumer brand.

assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay higher prices for a device they perceive as essential for survival.

Getinge can reach consumers through dedicated marketing and distribution channels.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Ottobock investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B offerings.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, or a viable path to capture value from individual buyers.
Any recommendation must consider Ottobock’s existing B2B revenue streams and current consumer reach (400 patient care centres).
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home use, fashion‑oriented prosthetics, or a new mobility solution) with a direct-to-consumer or partner channel.
2) Expand the existing B2B offerings by adding new features, services, or distribution channels without creating a separate consumer brand.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on current B2B markets (clinics, technicians, distributors, payers, and patient care centres).
4) Partner with or license Ottobock technology to third‑party consumer brands rather than creating a proprietary consumer brand.

predictions: In a test market, direct-to-consumer home-use sales will exceed B2B sales by at least 20% within 12 weeks.

X1.name: Consumer Proposition Test: Home vs. Premium Purchase Intent
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.
X1.sample: 500 respondents: 250 low-income (annual income < €30,000) and 250 high-income (annual income > €100,000) adults, recruited via panel providers.
X1.measure: 1) Purchase intent: binary (would buy) and WTP (maximum price). 2) Preference ranking: which product they would choose and why.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Low-income group will show higher purchase intent and WTP for home-use products than high-income group; high-income group will show higher intent for premium-priced products.
prediction_by_theory.T2: High-income group will show higher purchase intent and WTP for premium-priced products than low-income group; low-income group will show lower intent for premium-priced products.

X1.decision_rule: If low-income purchase intent exceeds high-income purchase intent by at least 15 percentage points, proceed to develop a differentiated home-use consumer proposition. If high-income purchase intent exceeds low-income purchase intent by at least 15 percentage points, proceed to develop a differentiated premium-priced consumer proposition. If both groups show similar intent, do not expand into a new consumer segment.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Public evidence shows Ottobock currently sells only to professionals and does not indicate consumer demand. A small-scale test (e.g., a willingness-to-pay survey) is needed to validate whether low-income patients would purchase home-use products.
final.target_customer: Low-income patients and their families who currently rely on clinic fees and manual fitting, as they face financial barriers to professional O&P services.
final.value_proposition: A differentiated home-use prosthetics/orthotics line that is affordable, easy to use, and delivered directly to patients, addressing the gap left by clinic fees and manual fitting.
final.next_action: Run the proposed 10-week willingness-to-pay survey test (500 respondents, €18,000) to measure purchase intent and price sensitivity across income groups.
final.uncertainty: The size of the low-income market for home-use products and whether they are willing to pay a premium compared to clinic-based options remain uncertain.
would_change_if: If the test shows low-income purchase intent exceeds high-income intent by at least 15 percentage points, we would proceed to develop a differentiated home-use consumer proposition.
If the test shows high-income purchase intent exceeds low-income intent by at least 15 percentage points, we would pursue a premium-priced consumer proposition.
If neither group shows a clear advantage, we would maintain the current B2B focus.

frame.objective: Determine whether Phoenix Contact should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current industrial, energy, and infrastructure products, and identify evidence that would justify that investment.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.

alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home solar PV control, home air‑conditioning automation).

T1.claim: Homeowners will purchase Phoenix Contact consumer products if they perceive the products as reliable, safety‑certified, and compatible with their existing home automation systems, because they need secure, fail‑safe connections for solar PV, HVAC, and other residential applications.
T1.who_benefits: Homeowners seeking reliable, safe, and compatible residential automation solutions.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: They are willing to pay a premium for products that offer proven industrial‑grade reliability and safety certification, reducing installation risk and maintenance costs.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Phoenix Contact can capture value through premium pricing, direct‑to‑consumer e‑commerce sales, and partnerships with residential automation retailers that emphasize safety and compatibility.
assumptions: Homeowners have sufficient budget to purchase premium automation components.
Safety certification and industrial reliability are key purchase drivers for residential applications.
Phoenix Contact can reach homeowners through existing distributor channels or direct sales.
predictions: In a test offering a safety‑certified terminal block marketed for solar PV, at least 30% of surveyed homeowners will express intent to purchase within 12 weeks.
Willingness to pay at least 20% above the price of a comparable non‑safety‑certified product.
T1.first_claim: Homeowners will purchase Phoenix Contact consumer products if they perceive the products as reliable, safety‑certified, and compatible with their existing home automation systems, because they need secure, fail‑safe connections for solar PV, HVAC, and other residential applications.

T2.claim: Homeowners will adopt Phoenix Contact consumer products if they perceive the products as part of a trusted, brand‑recognizable ecosystem that integrates with existing smart home platforms, because they value convenience and the promise of seamless integration.
T2.who_benefits: Homeowners who already use smart home devices and prefer brands they trust for reliability.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: They are willing to switch to a new brand if it offers a familiar interface, compatibility with their existing ecosystem, and the convenience of a single vendor for multiple home automation needs.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Phoenix Contact can capture value through premium pricing justified by brand trust, partnerships with smart home platform providers, and direct‑to‑consumer sales that highlight ecosystem compatibility.
assumptions: Smart home adoption rates among homeowners are sufficient to create a viable consumer market.
Brand recognition and trust are more important than price for this segment.
Phoenix Contact can leverage its existing industrial reputation to signal reliability to consumers.
predictions: In a test offering a terminal block marketed as compatible with a leading smart home platform, at least 25% of surveyed homeowners will express intent to purchase within 12 weeks.
Willingness to pay at least 15% above the price of a comparable non‑branded product.

X1.name: Consumer Proposition Test: Safety vs. Ecosystem Messaging
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging test. Participants are recruited from homeowners who have installed at least one smart home device. They are shown two identical product descriptions for a Phoenix Contact terminal block marketed for solar PV control: one emphasizes safety certification and industrial reliability; the other emphasizes compatibility with a leading smart home platform and brand recognition. Participants indicate purchase intent (yes/no) and maximum price they would pay. The test runs for 12 weeks with a 20% conversion threshold (e.g., at least 40% of participants indicating intent to purchase).
X1.sample: 500 homeowners who have installed at least one smart home device, recruited via an online panel. Stratified by region to ensure diversity.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (yes/no) and maximum price willingness to pay for each messaging variant.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Safety messaging will generate at least 40% purchase intent and a price premium of at least 20% over the non‑safety message.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Ecosystem messaging will generate at least 40% purchase intent and a price premium of at least 15% over the non‑ecosystem message.

X1.decision_rule: If safety messaging achieves ≥40% purchase intent and a ≥20% price premium, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition focused on safety certification. If ecosystem messaging achieves ≥40% purchase intent and a ≥15% price premium, proceed to develop a differentiated proposition focused on ecosystem compatibility. If neither condition is met, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition and continue focusing on industrial customers.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes safety certification and industrial reliability for residential solar PV and HVAC control, leveraging Phoenix Contact’s existing industrial reputation and safety credentials. Begin with a limited pilot offering the safety‑certified terminal block through an e‑commerce channel and partner with residential automation retailers to test demand and price.
final.target_customer: Homeowners who install residential solar PV systems, HVAC control systems, and other home automation devices, particularly those seeking reliable, fail‑safe connections.
final.value_proposition: A Phoenix Contact terminal block that meets safety certification and industrial standards, offering proven reliability and peace of mind for residential control applications, at a premium price justified by the product’s quality.
final.next_action: Run the proposed 12‑week, €18,000 online survey test with randomized messaging to measure purchase intent and price premium for safety‑certified versus ecosystem‑focused positioning.
final.uncertainty: The willingness of homeowners to pay a premium for safety certification and the size of the consumer market are uncertain. Evidence from the test will resolve whether T1 is supported or requires revision.
would_change_if: If the test shows purchase intent below 30% or a price premium below 15%, the investment would be reconsidered in favor of no expansion.
If new evidence shows strong consumer demand for ecosystem compatibility or brand recognition, the recommendation would shift toward an ecosystem‑focused proposition.

arguments.method: Online survey with randomized messaging test. Participants are recruited from homeowners who have installed at least one smart home device. They are shown two identical product descriptions for a Phoenix Contact terminal block marketed for solar PV control: one emphasizes safety certification and industrial reliability; the other emphasizes compatibility with a leading smart home platform and brand recognition. The test runs for 12 weeks with a 20% conversion threshold (e.g., at least 40% of participants indicating intent to purchase).
arguments.sample: 500 homeowners who have installed at least one smart home device, recruited via an online panel. Stratified by region to ensure diversity.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent (yes/no) and maximum price willingness to pay for each messaging variant.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Safety messaging will generate at least 40% purchase intent and a price premium of at least 20% over the non‑safety message.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Ecosystem messaging will generate at least 40% purchase intent and a price premium of at least 15% over the non‑ecosystem message.

arguments.decision_rule: If safety messaging achieves ≥40% purchase intent and a ≥20% price premium, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition focused on safety certification. If ecosystem messaging achieves ≥40% purchase intent and a ≥15% price premium, proceed to develop a differentiated proposition focused on ecosystem compatibility. If neither condition is met, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition and continue focusing on industrial customers.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

X1.name: Consumer Proposition Test: Online vs Retail Homeowner Lighting
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants are randomly assigned to either an online landing page (featuring Valmont's consumer proposition for outdoor lighting) or a retail store page (featuring the same proposition but framed as a retail product). Both pages include product description, price, durability claims, and a call to action to purchase. Participants indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and maximum price they would pay.
X1.sample: 500 homeowners (250 per arm) recruited via an online panel to match demographic distribution of target market (US, Canada, Europe).
X1.measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and maximum price willingness to pay for the Valmont outdoor lighting proposition.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay in the online arm (online demand theory).
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay in the retail arm (retail store theory).

X1.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent in the online arm exceeds the average purchase intent in the retail arm by at least 5 points (e.g., 7.5 vs 2.5), proceed to develop the online consumer proposition. If the difference is less than 5 points, conduct additional research on retail versus online channels before committing to a consumer proposition.

final.target_customer: Homeowners in the United States, Canada, and Europe who need reliable outdoor lighting for safety and convenience.
final.value_proposition: A direct-to-consumer online offering of durable, safety-compliant outdoor lighting products, leveraging Valmont’s existing manufacturing capacity and distribution network to offer premium pricing and quality.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer Proposition Test (X1) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for the online versus retail framing. If the online arm shows a 5‑point advantage, proceed to develop the online consumer proposition; if not,
final.uncertainty: The size of the consumer market for outdoor lighting and the willingness of homeowners to pay a premium for Valmont’s products are unknown. The test will resolve this uncertainty.
would_change_if: If the test shows the retail arm outperforms the online arm by at least 5 points, we would reconsider the consumer proposition and explore a retail-focused approach.

position.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes serviceability, reliability, and maintenance support for small contractors and homeowners, rather than premium branding. Use Metso’s existing dealer network and aftermarket service to deliver turnkey solutions that reduce downtime and operational risk.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Metso investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B offerings (aggregates plants, mobile units, automation, minerals processing, metals refining, aftermarket service).
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current customer base is quarries, contractors, mine maintenance and procurement staff, and mining/aggregates firms in 50+ countries.
Uncertainty about Metso’s current reach to individual buyers.
Any recommendation must be based on evidence of demand, willingness to pay, or competitive advantage that would generate value for Metso.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., homeowner DIY crushing for small-scale construction).
2) Expand the existing B2B offerings into adjacent consumer segments (e.g., small‑scale aggregate processing for residential developers).
3) No expansion – continue focusing exclusively on current B2B customer base and existing product portfolio.
4) Change the route to market or customer group (e.g., selling through online marketplaces or targeting a new segment of small businesses).
5) Redesign existing products for consumer use (e.g., modular crushing units for small quarries) without a new brand proposition.

T1.claim: Homeowners and small-scale contractors will adopt Metso crushing equipment if they perceive it as a reliable, serviceable product that reduces downtime and maintenance costs, because they lack the expertise to operate large crushers and prefer turnkey solutions.
T1.who_benefits: Small-scale contractors, residential developers, and individual homeowners who need aggregate processing for small projects.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: They would switch from renting or hiring to owning a Metso unit if the manufacturer provides easy access to service, training, and a warranty that minimizes operational risk.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Metso would capture value through premium pricing for a branded consumer unit, subscription services for maintenance, and distribution through its existing dealer network.
assumptions: Homeowners and small contractors currently rely on external operators for crushing.
They value reliability and serviceability more than cost alone.
Metso's service network can be adapted to serve individual buyers.
predictions: In a test offering a branded consumer crushing unit with service contracts, purchase intent among small contractors will be higher than among large contractors.
Surveyed homeowners will rank serviceability and warranty as the top reason for choosing Metso over competitors.
T1.first_claim: Homeowners and small-scale contractors will adopt Metso crushing equipment if they perceive it as a reliable, serviceable product that reduces downtime and maintenance costs, because they lack the expertise to operate large crushers and prefer turnkey solutions.

T2.claim: Homeowners and small contractors will adopt Metso crushing equipment if they perceive it as a premium, high-performance product that signals professional quality and durability, because they want to appear competent and reliable in their projects.
T2.who_benefits: Small contractors, residential developers, and homeowners who want to present a professional image and avoid reputational risk.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: They would choose Metso over generic brands if the product is marketed as a premium offering with advanced features, even if the price is higher.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Metso would capture value through premium pricing, brand positioning, and potential licensing of its technology to other consumer-facing brands.
assumptions: Consumers associate premium branding with superior performance.
Homeowners are willing to pay a premium for perceived quality.
Metso's brand can be extended to consumer markets without diluting its B2B reputation.
predictions: In a test offering a premium-branded consumer crushing unit, purchase intent among homeowners will be higher than among price-sensitive buyers.
Surveyed homeowners will rank brand prestige and performance as the top reasons for choosing Metso over competitors.
T2.first_claim: Homeowners and small contractors will adopt Metso crushing equipment if they perceive it as a premium, high-performance product that signals professional quality and durability, because they want to appear competent and reliable in their projects.

X1.name: Consumer Proposition Test: Service vs Premium Branding
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.
X1.sample: 300 respondents: 150 small contractors/residential developers and 150 homeowners, recruited via industry panels and homeowner forums.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy) and average WTP (EUR) for each brand proposition.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Small contractors will show higher purchase intent and WTP for a service-branded unit than homeowners, because they prioritize reliability and maintenance support.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Homeowners will show higher purchase intent and WTP for a premium-branded unit than small contractors, because they seek professional quality and brand prestige.

X1.decision_rule: If purchase intent among small contractors is at least 15 percentage points higher than among homeowners, proceed with a service-branded consumer proposition. If homeowners' intent is at least 15 points higher than small contractors, proceed with a premium-branded proposition. If neither difference is significant, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes serviceability, reliability, and maintenance support for small contractors and homeowners, leveraging Metso’s existing dealer network and aftermarket service.
final.target_customer: Small contractors, residential developers, and individual homeowners who need aggregate processing for small projects.
final.value_proposition: A turnkey crushing unit with easy access to service, training, and a warranty that minimizes downtime and operational risk, delivered through Metso’s trusted dealer network.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer Proposition Test (Service vs Premium Branding) to validate purchase intent and willingness-to-pay differences between small contractors and homeowners.
final.uncertainty: The size of the homeowner market and their willingness to pay for service-branded equipment is uncertain. Premium branding could also attract homeowners, but evidence of brand prestige demand is limited.
would_change_if: If the test shows homeowners’ purchase intent for a premium-branded unit is at least 15 percentage points higher than small contractors, we would shift focus to premium positioning.
If no significant difference is found, we would reconsider the investment in a differentiated consumer proposition.

frame.objective: Determine whether Victaulic should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B offerings, and identify evidence that would justify that investment.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current reach to individual buyers is unknown; must be discovered.
Any new proposition must be evaluated against existing distribution channels and current product portfolio.
Evidence must demonstrate consumer demand, willingness to pay, and feasibility of reaching individual buyers.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., homeowner plumbing, DIY sprinkler installation, or retail/commercial small‑project fittings).
2) Expand the existing distribution model to reach individual buyers directly through e‑commerce or retail partnerships without altering the product or pricing.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on B2B distribution to engineers, owners, contractors, and distributors.
4) Redesign existing products for consumer use (e.g., simplify packaging, add DIY instructions, or create a line of low‑cost, easy‑install fittings).
5) Partner with retailers or e‑commerce platforms to offer Victaulic products to individual consumers under a branded consumer line.

T1.claim: Homeowners and small‑project contractors will adopt Victaulic products if they perceive the products as reliable, easy to install, and safe for occupied spaces, because they value quick installation and minimal disruption to their projects.
T1.who_benefits: Homeowners and small‑project contractors who need fast, reliable plumbing and fire protection solutions without disrupting their living or working environment.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: They switch from generic or existing suppliers because they trust Victaulic's reputation for durability and safety, and because the products reduce installation time and risk of damage.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Victaulic would capture value by selling premium‑priced, branded consumer‑grade products through direct channels or retail partnerships, and by offering installation support or training to help consumers complete projects faster.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for proven reliability.
Installation time and disruption are significant pain points for homeowners and contractors.
Victaulic can reach consumers through existing distribution channels without major changes.
predictions: In a test offering a consumer‑focused line of flexible sprinkler fittings and grooved couplings, purchase intent among homeowners will be at least 15% higher than for a comparable generic product.
Consumers will report lower perceived installation time and disruption compared to competitors.
Sales conversion through e‑commerce or retail channels will be at least 5% of the test sample.

T2.why_behaviour_changes: They choose Victaulic over competitors because they trust its reputation for durability and safety, and because the products reduce long‑term maintenance and waste.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Victaulic would capture value by positioning its consumer‑grade products as eco‑friendly, offering certifications such as LEED compatibility, and selling through retail or e‑commerce channels that emphasize sustainability.
assumptions: Environmental concerns are a significant driver for homeowners and contractors in small projects.
Consumers are willing to pay a premium for eco‑friendly products.
Victaulic can obtain and communicate relevant sustainability certifications.
predictions: In a test offering a consumer‑focused line of eco‑friendly flexible sprinkler fittings and grooved couplings, purchase intent among environmentally conscious homeowners will be at least 20% higher than for a comparable generic product.
Consumers will report higher satisfaction with the product's environmental impact compared to competitors.
Sales conversion through eco‑focused retail or e‑commerce channels will be at least 10% of the test sample.

X1.name: Consumer Proposition Test: Reliability vs. Sustainability Messaging
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging test. Recruit 500 homeowners and small‑project contractors (n=250 per arm). Randomly assign participants to one of two product descriptions: Arm A (reliability focus) highlights quick, flame‑free installation and proven durability; Arm B (sustainability focus) emphasizes eco‑friendly materials, LEED compatibility, and reduced long‑term maintenance. Both arms include a product description, price, and a purchase decision question (yes/no). Track conversion rate and willingness to pay premium.
X1.sample: 500 participants (250 homeowners/small‑project contractors) recruited via an online panel, balanced across the two arms.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (yes/no) and willingness to pay a premium (EUR amount). Secondary measure: self‑reported importance of installation time/disruption (1‑7 scale).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Arm A conversion rate ≥ 15% and willingness to pay premium ≥ 10% of participants; Arm B conversion rate ≤ 10% and willingness to pay premium ≤ 5%.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Arm B conversion rate ≥ 20% and willingness to pay premium ≥ 10% of participants; Arm A conversion rate ≤ 10% and willingness to pay premium ≤ 5%.

X1.decision_rule: If Arm A conversion rate ≥ 15% and willingness to pay premium ≥ 10%, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition focused on reliability. If Arm B conversion rate ≥ 20% and willingness to pay premium ≥ 10%, develop a consumer proposition focused on sustainability. If neither arm meets its threshold, do not expand into consumer markets.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Victaulic already markets reliability and installation ease (victaulic-10), but public sources do not show consumer demand or willingness to pay a premium. Run the proposed reliability‑vs‑sustainability messaging test to validate whether reliability drives purchase intent before committing resources.
final.target_customer: Homeowners and small‑project contractors who need fast, reliable plumbing and fire protection solutions without disrupting their living or working environment.
final.value_proposition: A consumer‑grade line of Victaulic products that emphasizes quick, flame‑free installation and proven durability, sold through existing distribution channels or retail partnerships.
final.next_action: Execute the 12‑week, €18,000 online survey test comparing reliability‑focused and sustainability‑focused messaging, and apply the decision rule to decide whether to proceed with a consumer proposition.
final.uncertainty: The size of the consumer market, actual purchase intent, and willingness to pay a premium for Victaulic products are unknown. The test will resolve these uncertainties.
would_change_if: If the test shows a conversion rate below 15% or willingness to pay a premium below 10% for the reliability message, we would reconsider the consumer proposition.
If new evidence shows strong consumer demand for eco‑friendly products, we would shift focus to sustainability.
If a competitor launches a successful consumer line, we would reassess the competitive landscape.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Helmer Scientific investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current medical and lab equipment, parts, and disposables, sold via its online store to hospitals, labs, blood banks, and pharmacies.
constraints: Limited to publicly available information; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeframe for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must demonstrate consumer demand, willingness to pay, or a viable route to market for a differentiated consumer proposition.
Any recommendation must consider Helmer’s existing B2B focus and current reach to individual buyers.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual buyers (e.g., home refrigeration for small households) with a new product or service sold online.
2) Expand the existing B2B offerings by adding new medical or lab equipment categories or services without a consumer focus.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on hospitals, labs, blood banks, and pharmacies.
4) Partner with or license Helmer’s technology to third‑party consumer brands for co‑branded products.

X1.name: Consumer Messaging Test for Home Refrigeration
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from a panel of potential home consumers (n=300). Participants are randomly assigned to one of three message conditions: (1) Premium safety messaging emphasizing medical‑grade certification and trust for home use; (2) Safety messaging emphasizing protection of sensitive items (vaccines, medications) and repeat purchase of consumables; (3) Control condition with no messaging. Participants are asked to indicate willingness to purchase a Helmer‑branded home refrigerator at a price 20% above standard consumer refrigerators and to indicate intent to purchase a Helmer‑branded ice pack for vaccine storage at a price 15% above standard ice packs. The test is run in three 12‑week waves to capture conversion over time.
X1.sample: 300 potential home consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced across the three message conditions.
X1.measure: Primary outcome: percentage of participants in each condition who indicate willingness to purchase the Helmer‑branded home refrigerator at the premium price. Secondary outcome: repeat purchase intent for the Helmer‑branded ice pack.

prediction_by_theory.T1: At least 30% of participants in the premium safety condition will indicate willingness to purchase the home refrigerator at the premium price.
prediction_by_theory.T2: At least 25% of participants in the safety‑sensitive condition will indicate willingness to purchase the ice pack at the premium price.

X1.decision_rule: If the premium safety condition achieves at least 30% willingness to purchase the home refrigerator, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition for home refrigeration. If the safety‑sensitive condition achieves at least 25% willingness to purchase the ice pack, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition for sensitive item storage. If neither condition meets its threshold, do not invest in a consumer proposition and continue focusing on B2B offerings.

final.next_action: Conduct the proposed Consumer Messaging Test (X1) to measure willingness to purchase a premium, medical‑grade home refrigerator and an ice pack for vaccine storage. Use the decision rule to determine whether to proceed with a consumer brand
final.uncertainty: The size of the consumer market for premium home refrigeration and the actual willingness to pay a 20% premium are uncertain. The test will clarify these points before committing resources.
would_change_if: If the test shows at least 30% willingness to purchase the premium home refrigerator, we would recommend developing a differentiated consumer proposition for home refrigeration.
